analysis.evidence: With וַיּוֹצֵא אֹתוֹ ‘he brought him out’, הַחוּצָה tells where Abram was taken. The following command to look toward the sky and count the stars confirms the outdoor setting.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הַ precedes the masculine singular absolute noun חוּץ. The directional ending ־ָה marks the destination of the movement.

analysis.evidence: הַשָּׁמַיְמָה gives the direction of Abram’s gaze, toward the heavens. The following command וּסְפֹר הַכּוֹכָבִים, “and count the stars,” confirms the visual sense.
analysis.morphology: Hiphil imperative, second person masculine singular, addressed to Abram. The initial הַ is part of the verb form, and the dagesh in ב marks assimilation of the root-initial נ.

analysis.evidence: נָא immediately follows the imperative הַבֶּט, “look.” In הַבֶּט נָא הַשָּׁמַיְמָה, “please look toward the heavens,” it gives the command the force of an appeal.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew particle of entreaty, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: After bringing Abram outside, God tells him to look toward the sky and count the stars. The stars identify the visible sky as the object of his gaze.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הַ precedes a masculine plural noun in the absolute state. The final directional ה marks the sky as the goal of Abram’s gaze.

analysis.evidence: הַכּוֹכָבִים, “the stars,” is the object of the command. The speaker repeats the verb in אִם תּוּכַל לִסְפֹּר אֹתָם, “if you can count them.”
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וּ joins סְפֹר, a Qal masculine singular imperative addressed to Abram, to the preceding command הַבֶּט.

analysis.evidence: Abram is told to count the stars if he can. The words כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ, “so shall your offspring be,” use the number of visible stars as the measure of his future descendants.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הַ precedes a masculine plural noun in the absolute state.

analysis.evidence: After asking Abram to count the stars if he can, God says כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ, “So numerous will your offspring be.” The challenge to count the stars establishes the point of comparison.
analysis.morphology: An uninflected Hebrew demonstrative adverb with no prefix or suffix. It stands before יִהְיֶה and points back to the stars Abram has been asked to count.
analysis.sense: Thus, pointing to the number of the stars as the measure of Abram’s future descendants.

analysis.evidence: In כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ, ‘so will your offspring be’, כֹּה points back to the stars Abram is asked to count. The comparison describes how numerous his descendants will be.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, third person masculine singular, with future reference. It agrees with the masculine singular collective subject זַרְעֶךָ, ‘your offspring’.

analysis.evidence: God asks Abram to count the stars if he can, then says כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ, “So shall your descendants be.” כֹּה points back to the multitude of stars, expressing how numerous God promises Abram’s descendants will be.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix referring to Abram. The singular noun denotes his descendants collectively.
